title: The essay as a practice
hookLine: an essay is a trying-out, and so is a life

lines: TOO DEEP: BACK TO THE BANK.
cards: A river with no bridge. You want to cross, but you can't see the bottom. So you push a long stick in, a little way out from the bank.
Shallow. A little farther. Still fine.
Farther, and the stick disappears and keeps going. You step back onto the bank. Nobody calls that failure; you found out where the bottom was.
Montaigne uses almost that exact picture for how he puts his judgment to work. Today, the name he gave the whole thing.

teach.h: SOUND THE FORD FROM FAR OFF.
teach.b: First, the ford. In an early essay, Montaigne says judgment is a tool for every subject, and he tries it on all of them, even ones he doesn't understand. He sounds the ford from far off.
If it's too deep for his height, he stays on the bank. And knowing he can't cross is itself something his judgment learned. Second, the word.

He called his book Essais, and in the essay Of repentance he tells us what he means, roughly: if my mind could find firm footing, I wouldn't be essaying myself, trying myself out; I'd be making up my mind.
But it's always in apprenticeship and on trial.
So the essays aren't verdicts. They're tests, with himself as the material. Third, what that frees him to do.
A trial can fail and still teach. He can try out an opinion on Monday and its opposite on Thursday, and both go in the book. He isn't building a system; he's checking the depth, stick in hand.
Fourth, the life. Read that way, an essay is less a school assignment and more a practice.
Try a thought, a habit, a kinder answer to someone who annoys you. Too deep: back to the bank, no shame. If it holds, take another step.
Big, frozen decisions become small experiments you can actually begin.

how: Readers often take Montaigne's own play on the word essais, trials or attempts, as a way of living: trying out thoughts and habits as experiments rather than settling everything at once.

games.q: what does “the essay as a practice” mean?
o: Montaigne's essays as trials: trying a thought, not a verdict
a formal speech given to defend a fixed position
a school assignment graded on its length and neatness

games.q: inside the essay as a practice: tap the pairs.
p: testing the depth from the bank

s: Montaigne meant his essays as final verdicts
he says his mind is always in apprenticeship and on trial; essays, not decisions.
he says knowing a ford is too deep is something judgment learns
staying on the bank is part of what the trial teaches.
he only tried his judgment on subjects he knew well
he tries it on every subject, even ones he doesn't understand.

games.q: you're Montaigne at the river. you push the stick in, and it's deeper than you are tall. what does he say he does?
o: stay on the bank, and count that as something learned.
games.why: he stays on the bank. knowing he can't cross is itself something his judgment learned from the trial.

practice: Bring to mind a decision you've been treating as huge and final, and shrink it into a trial: not quit the job, but ask one question; not change everything, but one different breakfast, one different reply.
Choose the smallest version that would still tell you something, and picture pushing the stick in, just a little way.

wordCard.voice: The essay as a practice. Montaigne's Essais are trials, tryings-out, a mind always on trial, never quite settled into decisions. Today's word.

orig.note: Montaigne's French title, written in the Latin alphabet: trials, attempts.

carryVoice: Your line: a trying-out. A trial that fails still tells you where the bottom is. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Essays 1.50, Of Democritus and Heraclitus (judgment as a tool for every subject; sounding the ford from far off and staying on the bank)
Essays 3.2, Of repentance (if his mind could find firm footing he would not make essays but decisions; it is always in apprenticeship and on trial)
